In 1837 Michael Faraday found that sliding a nonconducting material — a dielectric — into the gap increases the capacitance. The experiment is worth stating precisely, because the bookkeeping depends on how it is done.

Charge a capacitor to \(\Delta V_0\), disconnect the battery so that \(Q\) is fixed, then insert the dielectric. The voltage falls, to \(\Delta V_0/\kappa\), where \(\kappa \ge 1\) is the dielectric constant of the material. Since \(Q\) did not change and \(\Delta V\) fell by \(\kappa\):

\[\boxed{\;C = \kappa C_0\;} \qquad\text{and for parallel plates}\qquad \boxed{\;C = \frac{\kappa\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\;}\]

Material \(\kappa\) Dielectric strength (\(10^6\) V/m)
Vacuum 1.00000 —
Air 1.00059 3
Teflon 2.1 60
Paper 3.7 16
Glass (Pyrex) 5.6 14
Water 80 —
Strontium titanate 233 8

Why a Dielectric Increases Capacitance

The mechanism is polarization. Place an insulator in a field and its charge cannot flow — but it can shift.

  • Polar molecules already carry a permanent dipole moment. The field exerts a torque that rotates them into alignment.
  • Nonpolar molecules have no permanent dipole, but the field pulls their electron clouds one way and nuclei the other, inducing one.

Either way the material ends up with aligned dipoles: a layer of negative charge facing the positive plate, positive facing the negative plate. Those surface layers produce a field opposing the original, so the net field drops:

\[E = \frac{E_0}{\kappa}\]

A weaker field means a smaller \(\Delta V\) across the same gap, and a smaller \(\Delta V\) for the same \(Q\) means a larger \(C\). It is convenient to fold \(\kappa\) into a permittivity \(\varepsilon = \kappa\varepsilon_0\), so that \(C = \varepsilon A/d\) and the vacuum case is just \(\kappa = 1\).

Two Scenarios, and They Differ

Everything depends on whether the battery is still attached.

Quantity Battery connected (\(\Delta V\) fixed) Battery disconnected (\(Q\) fixed)
Capacitance \(C\) \(\times\kappa\) \(\times\kappa\)
Charge \(Q\) \(\times\kappa\) unchanged
Voltage \(\Delta V\) unchanged \(\div\kappa\)
Energy \(U\) \(\times\kappa\) \(\div\kappa\)

The energy column is the one to think about, because it moves in opposite directions.

Battery connected: \(U = \tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2\) with \(\Delta V\) held fixed and \(C\) up by \(\kappa\), so \(U\) rises. The battery supplied the extra energy — it pushed additional charge onto the plates to maintain the voltage.

Battery disconnected: \(U = Q^2/2C\) with \(Q\) held fixed and \(C\) up by \(\kappa\), so \(U\) falls. Nothing is missing: the capacitor did work on the dielectric. The fringing field at the edge of the gap pulls the slab inward, and the energy lost from the field went into that mechanical work. Let go of a dielectric slab near a charged capacitor and it is drawn in — that is the same energy, visible.

The table is not something to memorise — every row comes from one chain. Name what the circuit holds fixed, let \(C = \kappa C_0\) change, and get the free variable from \(Q = C\Delta V\). Then write the energy in the form whose variable is fixed, so that only \(C\) moves.

One Slab, Two Circuits

An empty \(C_0 = 200\) pF capacitor is charged from a \(40.0\) V battery. A slab with \(\kappa = 4.0\) — about silicon dioxide (\(\kappa \approx 3.9\)), the glass insulating layer inside nearly every transistor — is then slid into the gap, once with the battery still connected and once after disconnecting it first.

Before the slab, both cases start from the same numbers:

\[Q_0 = C_0\Delta V_0 = (200\ \text{pF})(40.0\ \text{V}) = 8.00\ \text{nC} \qquad U_0 = \frac{1}{2}C_0\Delta V_0^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(200\ \text{pF})(40.0\ \text{V})^{2} = 160\ \text{nJ}\]

Step 1 — what is fixed. Connected, the battery holds \(\Delta V = 40.0\) V. Disconnected, no path leads on or off the plates, so \(Q = 8.00\) nC is trapped.

Step 2 — the capacitance. \(C\) depends only on geometry and material, so it is the same in both cases:

\[C = \kappa C_0 = 4.0\,(200\ \text{pF}) = 800\ \text{pF}\]

Step 3 — the free variable, from \(Q = C\Delta V\).

\[\text{connected:}\quad Q = C\Delta V = (800\ \text{pF})(40.0\ \text{V}) = 32.0\ \text{nC} \qquad\qquad \text{disconnected:}\quad \Delta V = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{8.00\ \text{nC}}{800\ \text{pF}} = 10.0\ \text{V}\]

Step 4 — the energy, in the form whose variable is fixed.

\[\text{connected:}\quad U = \frac{1}{2}C\Delta V^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(800\ \text{pF})(40.0\ \text{V})^{2} = 640\ \text{nJ} \qquad\qquad \text{disconnected:}\quad U = \frac{Q^{2}}{2C} = \frac{(8.00\ \text{nC})^{2}}{2(800\ \text{pF})} = 40.0\ \text{nJ}\]

Battery connected Battery disconnected
fixed \(\Delta V = 40.0\) V \(Q = 8.00\) nC
\(C\) \(800\) pF (\(\times\kappa\)) \(800\) pF (\(\times\kappa\))
\(Q\) \(32.0\) nC (\(\times\kappa\)) \(8.00\) nC (unchanged)
\(\Delta V\) \(40.0\) V (unchanged) \(10.0\) V (\(\div\kappa\))
\(U\) \(640\) nJ (\(\times\kappa\)) \(40.0\) nJ (\(\div\kappa\))

\[\boxed{\;\text{Same slab, same } C = 800\ \text{pF}: \ U \text{ up by } \kappa \text{ connected, down by } \kappa \text{ disconnected.}\;}\]

Follow the energy in both columns. Disconnected, the field lost \(160 - 40 = 120\) nJ, and that is the work it did pulling the slab in. Connected, the battery pushed an extra \(32.0 - 8.00 = 24.0\) nC through \(40.0\) V, which is \(W_{\text{bat}} = (24.0\ \text{nC})(40.0\ \text{V}) = 960\) nJ. Only \(640 - 160 = 480\) nJ of that stayed in the field. The other \(480\) nJ is again the work done pulling the slab in: the slab is drawn in either way, and the battery pays for it as well as for the stored energy.

Dielectric Strength and Breakdown

Every insulator fails at a large enough field. Beyond its dielectric strength, the material ionises and suddenly conducts — a spark, an arc, or on the largest scale, lightning. The maximum voltage a capacitor can hold is

\[\Delta V_{\text{max}} = E_{\text{max}}\,d\]

A dielectric earns its place twice over. It multiplies \(C\) by \(\kappa\), and because its dielectric strength usually exceeds air’s \(3\times10^6\) V/m, it also raises \(\Delta V_{\text{max}}\). Teflon does both aggressively: \(\kappa = 2.1\) with a strength of \(60\times10^6\) V/m, twenty times air’s.

This is also why \(d \to 0\) does not really give \(C \to \infty\) (§25.2). Shrinking the gap raises the field at fixed voltage, and the material breaks down first.

Fill the same \(1.00\) mm gap two ways:

\(\kappa\) \(E_{\text{max}}\) \(\Delta V_{\text{max}} = E_{\text{max}}d\)
air \(1.00\) \(3\times10^{6}\) V/m \(3.0\) kV
strontium titanate \(233\) \(8\times10^{6}\) V/m \(8.0\) kV

The capacitance rises by \(233\) and the voltage limit by \(8/3 \approx 2.7\). The most energy the capacitor can hold, \(U_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}C\Delta V_{\max}^{2}\), takes the first factor once and the second squared: \(233\times(8/3)^{2} \approx 1700\).

Partially Filled Gaps

A slab that fills only part of the gap is not a special case needing new physics — it is two capacitors, and §25.4 already says how to combine them. The only question is which rule applies, and the answer is decided by how the slab is placed.

Stacked (one above the other). Each layer spans the full plate area \(A\) but only part of the separation. They share the same charge, so they are in series:

\[C_i = \frac{\kappa_i\varepsilon_0 A}{d_i}, \qquad \frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}\]

Side by side (each covering part of the area). Each slab spans the full separation \(d\) but only part of the area. They share the same voltage, so they are in parallel:

\[C_i = \frac{\kappa_i\varepsilon_0 A_i}{d}, \qquad C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2\]

The stacked case is the dangerous one, and the figure shows why. With \(\kappa = 4.0\) filling the lower half, the two layers carry the same charge, so the smaller capacitance takes the larger share of the voltage — and the air layer, with \(\kappa = 1\), is the smaller one. It absorbs \(80\) of the \(100\) V across half the gap, giving it four times the field inside the slab.

So the air breaks down first, at a total voltage well below what the dielectric alone could withstand. A gap that is partly air is limited by the air, which is why capacitors are built with the dielectric filling the gap completely and why a trapped bubble is a manufacturing defect rather than a cosmetic one.

Side by side, nothing of the sort happens: both halves see the same \(\Delta V\) across the same \(d\), so both see the same field, and the one with the larger \(\kappa\) simply stores proportionally more charge.

Half Air, Half \(\kappa = 3\), Two Ways

The same two materials, arranged both ways — and each arrangement worked by two routes. Work in units of the empty capacitor, \(C_0 = \varepsilon_0A/d\), which holds \(Q_0\) at \(\Delta V_0 = E_0d\).

  • Geometry: cut the gap into two capacitors, find each from \(C = \kappa\varepsilon_0A_i/d_i\), and combine them with the rules of §25.4.
  • Fields and voltages: compare with the empty capacitor, and apply the two-scenario table above to part of the gap. Pieces that share \(Q\) follow the disconnected column (field and voltage \(\div\kappa\)); pieces that share \(\Delta V\) follow the connected column (charge \(\times\kappa\)).

Stacked — each layer spans all of \(A\) but only \(d/2\). Why series: slide an imaginary thin metal sheet along the boundary. The field meets it at right angles, so it changes nothing — and it is an isolated conductor, like the middle plates of §25.4, so the two layers carry the same \(Q\).

Geometry.

\[C_{\text{air}} = \frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d/2} = 2C_0 \qquad C_{\kappa} = 3(2C_0) = 6C_0 \qquad \frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{2C_0}+\frac{1}{6C_0} \;\Rightarrow\; C = 1.5\,C_0\]

Same \(Q\), so \(\Delta V_i = Q/C_i\): the air layer takes three times the voltage of the slab, \(\frac{3}{4}\Delta V\) against \(\frac{1}{4}\Delta V\), and the fields follow last,

\[E_{\text{air}} = \frac{\frac{3}{4}\Delta V}{d/2} = 1.5\,\frac{\Delta V}{d} \qquad E_{\kappa} = \frac{\frac{1}{4}\Delta V}{d/2} = 0.5\,\frac{\Delta V}{d} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \frac{E_{\text{air}}}{E_\kappa} = \kappa\]

Fields and voltages. Both layers sit between the same \(\pm Q_0\) as the empty capacitor. The air layer has the empty capacitor’s field; the slab layer is the disconnected case, its field reduced by \(\kappa\):

\[E_{\text{air}} = E_0 \qquad E_\kappa = \frac{E_0}{3} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \frac{E_{\text{air}}}{E_\kappa} = \kappa\]

Each layer is \(d/2\) thick, so the voltage split is the field ratio:

\[E_{\text{air}}\frac{d}{2} : E_\kappa\frac{d}{2} = 3 : 1 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \tfrac{3}{4}\Delta V \text{ and } \tfrac{1}{4}\Delta V\]

Adding the two layers gives the total, and \(C\) comes last:

\[\Delta V = E_0\frac{d}{2} + \frac{E_0}{3}\frac{d}{2} = \frac{2}{3}E_0d = \frac{2}{3}\Delta V_0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad C = \frac{Q_0}{\frac{2}{3}\Delta V_0} = 1.5\,C_0\]

The two routes reach the same place in opposite order — geometry finds \(C\) first and the fields last; fields and voltages finds the fields first and \(C\) last. Either way the weak layer carries the strong field, and it is the one that breaks down first.

Side by side — each half spans all of \(d\) but only \(A/2\). Why parallel: both halves touch the same two plates, and each plate is one conductor at one potential, so the halves share \(\Delta V\) — and, spanning the same \(d\), the same field \(\Delta V/d\).

Geometry.

\[C_{\text{air}} = \frac{\varepsilon_0(A/2)}{d} = \frac{1}{2}C_0 \qquad C_{\kappa} = 3\left(\frac{1}{2}C_0\right) = \frac{3}{2}C_0 \qquad C = \frac{1}{2}C_0 + \frac{3}{2}C_0 = 2\,C_0\]

Same \(\Delta V\), so \(Q_i = C_i\Delta V\), and the charges follow last: \(Q_\kappa/Q_{\text{air}} = (3/2)/(1/2) = \kappa\).

Fields and voltages. Hold the empty capacitor’s \(\Delta V_0\). The air half carries what that half of the empty capacitor would, \(Q_0/2\); the slab half is the connected case, its charge raised by \(\kappa\):

\[Q_{\text{air}} = \frac{Q_0}{2} \qquad Q_\kappa = 3\cdot\frac{Q_0}{2} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \frac{Q_\kappa}{Q_{\text{air}}} = \kappa \qquad\qquad C = \frac{\frac{1}{2}Q_0 + \frac{3}{2}Q_0}{\Delta V_0} = 2\,C_0\]

Twice the charge at the same voltage. The charge on each plate is not uniform — it is three times denser over the slab — which a conductor is free to arrange.

shared by the two pieces column of the table so \(\kappa\) shows up in
stacked (series) \(Q\) disconnected the field: \(E_{\text{air}}/E_\kappa = \kappa\)
side by side (parallel) \(\Delta V\), so \(E\) connected the charge: \(Q_\kappa/Q_{\text{air}} = \kappa\)

\[\boxed{\;\text{Same materials: stacked } C = 1.5\,C_0 \text{ (series)}, \qquad \text{side by side } C = 2\,C_0 \text{ (parallel).}\;}\]

Bound-check both. Series: \(1.5\,C_0\) is below the smallest member, \(2\,C_0\) ✓. Parallel: \(2\,C_0\) is above the largest member, \(1.5\,C_0\) ✓.

Whichever the pieces share, the other quantity carries the factor \(\kappa\): share \(Q\) and the fields differ by \(\kappa\); share \(\Delta V\) and the charges do.

Why the two-scenario table works at all. Combine the parallel-plate field \(E_0 = \sigma/\varepsilon_0\) with the polarization result \(E = E_0/\kappa\): the free charge density on a plate and the field beside it are tied by \(\sigma = \kappa\varepsilon_0E\). Fix \(\sigma\) and \(E\) carries the \(\kappa\); fix \(E\) and \(\sigma\) carries it. Both columns of the table, and both halves of this example, are that one relation.

Inserting a Dielectric

\(C_0 = 100\) pF is charged to \(\Delta V_0 = 50.0\) V. The battery is then disconnected, and a slab with \(\kappa = 5.0\) is inserted.

Before insertion, the charge is fixed at

\[Q = C_0\Delta V_0 = (100\times10^{-12})(50.0) = 5.00\ \text{nC}\]

(a) The new capacitance. \(C = \kappa C_0 = 5.0(100) = 500\) pF.

(b) The new voltage. \(Q\) is unchanged, so

\[\Delta V = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{5.00\times10^{-9}}{500\times10^{-12}} = 10.0\ \text{V}\]

(c) The energies.

\[U_0 = \frac{Q^2}{2C_0} = 125\ \text{nJ}, \qquad U = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = 25.0\ \text{nJ}\]

\[\boxed{\;C = 500\ \text{pF}, \qquad \Delta V = 10.0\ \text{V}, \qquad \frac{U}{U_0} = \frac{1}{\kappa} = \frac{1}{5}\;}\]

The voltage fell by exactly \(\kappa\) and the energy by exactly \(\kappa\), both as the table predicts. The missing \(100\) nJ is not lost — it is the work the fringing field did pulling the slab into the gap. Had the battery stayed connected instead, every entry in this example would differ, and the energy would have gone up by a factor of five.

Electric Dipoles in a Field

The polarization argument rests on dipoles turning, so it is worth writing down what a field does to one. For a dipole \(\vec p = q\vec d\) in a uniform field, the two forces are equal and opposite — no net force — but they act at different points, so they produce a torque:

\[\boxed{\;\vec\tau = \vec p \times \vec E \qquad\qquad U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E = -pE\cos\theta\;}\]

The energy is minimum when \(\vec p\) is parallel to \(\vec E\) — the stable alignment — and maximum when antiparallel. In a non-uniform field the two forces no longer cancel, and the dipole is pulled toward the stronger field. That is the force that drags a dielectric slab into a capacitor gap.

These two expressions return almost unchanged for magnetic dipoles in Chapter 28: \(\vec\tau = \vec\mu\times\vec B\) and \(U = -\vec\mu\cdot\vec B\). Same mathematics, different letters — worth noticing now so that it costs nothing later.
